bull_thesis: Tencent Music is China's dominant music-streaming and social-entertainment platform, majority-owned by Tencent, and it is being handed to us cheap after a brutal wash-out — the stock is down roughly two-thirds from its 52-week high near HK$104 to the mid-HK$30s. The screener's headline that this is 96% overvalued is a units error: mixing the company's renminbi financials against a mis-scaled price. The real math is the opposite. On live market data the shares trade near 8-9 times forward earnings, and the balance sheet holds roughly RMB 41 billion of cash and investments (about RMB 22 billion of pure net cash after debt) against a market value near RMB 103 billion — so a quarter of the price is cash. Strip that out and the operating business trades around 9-10 times clean earnings for a franchise with 57% gross margins, ~34% net margins and free-cash-flow conversion above 30% — profitability Western streamers like Spotify or the record majors cannot touch, driven by the China karaoke and live-streaming mix. Management has done what it said for three straight years: net income more than tripled from RMB 3.03 billion in 2021 to RMB 10.77 billion in 2025 on roughly flat revenue, exactly the 'cost grows slower than revenue' promise kept. Capital returns are real and rising — a meaningfully larger 2025 dividend plus a fresh US$1 billion, two-year buyback, easily funded by the cash pile. Subscription and advertising keep compounding, Super VIP crossed 15 million members, and a new concert-and-merchandise 'fan economy' engine (the G-Dragon world tour drew 260,000 fans across eight Asian cities) is opening a larger addressable market. For this to work you mainly need the generative-AI threat to the royalty pool to stay a manageable-to-material risk rather than turning terminal, and rational competition in Chinese streaming to hold.
bear_thesis: The re-rating driver is already spent and the growth engine is cooling. The one live catalyst in the file — the Ximalaya audio-platform acquisition, which management on the March 2026 call could only say it was 'still communicating with the regulator' about — has since fired: China's market regulator cleared it on 12 May 2026 and the deal closed on 18 May 2026, but only under five behavioral conditions that cut the wrong way, forcing Tencent Music to give up exclusive audio-licensing rights, hold prices, keep free content generous, and stop blocking creators from rival platforms. That is a direct attack on the exclusivity that would have widened the moat, and the re-rate from the deal is behind us. Meanwhile growth is decelerating hard: first-quarter 2026 revenue rose just 7.3% (down from ~13% in 2025), non-IFRS profit rose only 7%, and social entertainment fell another 11%. The fiscal-2025 earnings-per-share surge of ~64% that made this look explosive is partly a one-off disposal gain — the most recent quarter's earnings per share actually fell about 52% year-over-year, and trailing-twelve-month diluted earnings (RMB 2.84) sit below the annual headline (RMB 3.47). Management just announced it will stop disclosing quarterly subscriber and revenue-per-user metrics, reducing transparency exactly as the core engine matures. And the terminal question is unresolved: analysts pressed directly on whether AI-generated music erodes the royalty pool, and management answered with conviction, not data. Returns are only middling — return on equity ~9%, return on invested capital ~8.7%. What confirms the bear: another quarter of sub-8% revenue growth, a further margin walk-down (2026 gross margin already guided flat-to-lower), or evidence AI content is displacing licensed catalog streams.

valley_of_death: The next three-to-nine months carry no cash-burn or maturity risk — the company is net cash and free-cash-flow positive, so there is no balance-sheet cliff. Any of these can keep the stock in a mid-HK$30s range and re-test the lows even though the fundamentals are fine — a slow grind rather than a flush.
positioning_washout: The two-thirds drawdown from the HK$104 high to the mid-HK$30s has already done much of the forced selling — momentum and growth funds that owned it near the highs have largely capitulated, which is part of why it is cheap. If anything the shareholder base has already rotated from growth toward value hands, which is a cleaner setup, but it also means there is no imminent capitulation event to buy into at a lower price — the wash-out is mostly behind, not ahead.
moderator_conclusion: This is a good business at a cheap price with its catalyst already behind it — a value case, not a special-situation trade. Take away about RMB 13.8 billion of net cash (cash RMB 30.7 billion less RMB 16.9 billion of debt at 30 June 2026) and the operating business is priced near RMB 72 billion - about 9 times clean earnings of RMB 8 billion. That is a single-digit multiple for a platform with a 57% gross margin, a ~34% net margin and a free-cash-flow margin of ~31% (free cash flow is the cash left after running and investing in the business; RMB 8.9 billion over the trailing twelve months, TTM). Management has a record of keeping its word: it promised in 2025 that 'cost growth is always lower than revenue growth', and net income more than tripled from RMB 3.0 billion in 2021 to RMB 10.8 billion in 2025 on flat revenue. Capital returns are real and growing: US$400 million of shares were repurchased in the second quarter of 2026 alone under a US$1 billion programme, and on 2026-08-11 management said it is 'preparing for another round of share buyback'. Analysts on that call pointed out that cash and deposits of about RMB 44 billion equal close to 40% of the market value. The content base is secure - multi-year renewals with Sony (2025) and Warner (Q4-2025) plus deeper label partnerships in Q2-2026 - and the concerts-and-merchandise line keeps growing. The stock is down about two-thirds from its 52-week high of HK$91.55 and only 8% above its 52-week low of HK$30.36, so a lot of bad news is in the price. Conditions for the bull case: revenue growth holds at mid-single digits, gross margin dips only modestly as guided, and buybacks continue at single-digit multiples.
bear_thesis: Growth is fading while competition and technology turn against the franchise. Revenue growth slowed from about 13% in 2025 to 5.8% in Q2-2026 (RMB 8.93 billion, reported 2026-08-11), and that figure includes the first consolidation of Ximalaya, so organic growth was lower still; social entertainment (karaoke and live streaming) shrank about 17% year on year. On the same call management guided second-half gross margin 'decreasing slightly year-over-year', sales spending 'up a little bit' and the full-year net margin 'down slightly'. A short-video giant (ByteDance's Soda Music) is competing for casual listeners, and the company no longer headlines the quarterly paying-user and revenue-per-user numbers that would reveal share loss early. The 2025 earnings surge (EPS RMB 3.47, +64%) included a one-off gain; TTM diluted EPS to June 2026 is RMB 2.84 and the latest quarter's EPS was flat year on year. The balance sheet is no longer pure cash: debt rose from RMB 4.8 billion to RMB 16.9 billion in Q2-2026 to help pay for Ximalaya, and a further US$1 billion of notes (5.05% due 2031, 5.65% due 2036) closed on 2026-09-10. The regulator bars exclusive content deals, so Ximalaya cannot be used to lock users in. Generative AI is an unresolved threat to the value of licensed catalogues and to pricing power. Return on invested capital is a moderate ~8.7%. If clean earnings slip toward RMB 7 billion and the market keeps paying about 9 times, the shares are worth about HK$29, below today's price, and the China-internet discount means no date forces a re-rating.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the price implies a business in structural decline. At HK$32.84 the operating business, net of RMB 13.8 billion of net cash, is valued at about 9 times clean earnings - a multiple usually reserved for shrinking franchises. The evidence so far says otherwise: Q2-2026 attributable profit was RMB 2.5 billion against 2.4 billion a year earlier, revenue still grew about 6%, margins sit near record levels and TTM free cash flow of about RMB 8.9 billion funds a rising dividend and buybacks (US$400 million in Q2-2026 alone, with another programme being prepared). Q2-2026 earnings modestly beat estimates (US$0.25 per ADS against US$0.24, FMP). Brokers are mostly neutral (13 firms, 10 hold and 3 buy, per a MarketBeat tally of 2026-08-31, carried from prior coverage). What we concede: organic growth is genuinely decelerating, the competition and AI threats cannot be measured with the reduced disclosure, and much of the de-rating is shared with other Chinese internet names, so the stock deserves a below-peer multiple rather than a return to its old highs.
forcing_function: The nearest dated event is the Q3-2026 results, dated 2026-11-17 (company-confirmed 2026-10-13): the first full quarter with Ximalaya and the first balance sheet after the US$1 billion bond. It will show whether revenue growth holds near 5% and gross margin holds. Beyond that, the re-rating is self-generated: a second buyback programme that management said on 2026-08-11 it is preparing, the annual dividend with Q4 results around March 2027, and continued share-count reduction at a single-digit multiple. The Ximalaya acquisition itself has already happened.
valley_of_death: The risky window (the months just ahead) is the Q3-2026 report on 2026-11-17 and the Q4 print around March 2027. There is no solvency risk - the company is net cash, cash generative, and its new bonds mature in 2031 and 2036. The danger is narrative: organic revenue growth below 5%, a further gross-margin step-down as concerts and merchandise grow, or higher marketing spend to defend users against short-video competition. With quarterly user data no longer headlined, the market will assume the worst on any miss. A higher-rate global tape does not reward slow-growth foreign-listed names. The shares sit only 8% above their 52-week low and could revisit it into the print.
positioning_washout: Little forced-selling pressure is left. The stock is down about two-thirds from its 52-week high and about 24% below its 200-day average; growth and momentum holders have largely gone, and institutional trimming has been visible through 2026. No dividend cut, index deletion or lock-up expiry is pending that would trigger new forced selling. The remaining risk is slow drift by China-internet allocators, not a capitulation event to buy into - which is why the committee waits for proof rather than for a lower price.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for proof: we buy once the Q3-2026 report confirms revenue growth at or above about 5% with gross margin holding and net cash intact, due 2026-11-17. This is unchanged from last week's call (conviction 3, value score 4); the only change since then is the price, HK$33.50; the test date stays company-confirmed for 2026-11-17. On value the case is strong: about 9 times clean earnings excluding net cash, a base-case fair value near HK$43 - about 28% above today's price, comfortably more than the 20% discount we require in today's reflationary backdrop - and a management team that has kept its margin and capital-return promises. The thesis is in doubt until the Q3 report because the growth half of it is weakening: revenue growth slowed from about 13% in 2025 to under 6% organically in Q2-2026, gross margin is guided slightly lower in the second half, and the company no longer headlines the user data that would show whether a short-video rival is taking share. The value score stops at 4 because durability, not price, is the missing ingredient: the generative-AI threat to licensed music and pricing power is unresolved. The Ximalaya acquisition has already happened, so there is no event edge here; we judge the residual value, which is real. If Q3 passes, the thesis holds and the discount qualifies as a buy at today's price; if revenue turns down or margin drops sharply, the thesis has broken and we pass.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that this is a high-quality franchise priced for a decline that is not happening, and that one number has been hiding it. Group revenue looked flat for three years - RMB 31.2 billion in 2021, RMB 28.3 billion in 2022, RMB 27.8 billion in 2023, RMB 28.4 billion in 2024 - which is why our own screener shows a three-year revenue growth rate of just 4.2%. But the company's segment disclosure shows two opposite businesses inside that flat line. Online music services (subscriptions and advertising) grew from RMB 12.5 billion in 2022 to RMB 26.7 billion in 2025, compounding at about 29% a year. Over the same period the old live-streaming and virtual-gifting business shrank from roughly RMB 15.9 billion to roughly RMB 5.3 billion, a two-thirds collapse under China's 2021 crackdown on tipping. The shrinking business is now only about 15% of revenue, so the drag that suppressed reported growth for three years is nearly exhausted, and group growth should converge upward toward the music engine rather than downward. In 2025 that convergence showed up: revenue +12.8% and online music +22.9%.

The second leg is cash. At 2026-06-30 cash and short-term investments were RMB 30.7 billion against total debt of RMB 16.9 billion - genuine net cash of RMB 13.8 billion, about 14% of the market value. Management went further on the 2026-08-11 call, saying "total cash, short-term long-term deposit reached RMB 44 billion" and that this was "almost 40% of our current market cap", which implies roughly another RMB 13 billion of longer-dated deposits that a simple net-cash calculation misses. Cash conversion is real too: trailing operating cash flow of about RMB 11.2 billion against net income of RMB 8.6 billion, better than one-for-one. On the 2026-08-11 call the company confirmed it "already completed USD 400 million share buyback" in the quarter and is "preparing for another round".

The third leg is that the new engine is working. Live concerts and artist merchandise have gone from a side activity to a scaled business: a 20-show G-Dragon world tour across eight Asia-Pacific cities drawing "over 260,000 fans" (2026-03-17), a proprietary awards-concert brand moved into a Hong Kong stadium with capacity up more than threefold (2026-08-11), and management saying it "more than doubled revenues of IP-related merchandise and fan-based consumption" in 2025. These are exactly the parts of music consumption that generative artificial intelligence cannot synthesise, which is the bull answer to the biggest terminal-value fear in the stock.

Finally, the price. The shares are roughly 57% below their 52-week high of HK$86.45, at about 11 times trailing earnings and under 11 times once net cash is stripped out, for a business with 44% gross margins, 34% operating margins and the Tencent group's distribution behind it. The conditions the bull case needs are narrow and checkable: organic revenue growth re-accelerating to mid-single digits or better once Ximalaya is in the base, gross margin holding near 44%, and the cash being returned rather than spent on more acquisitions.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the cheapness is measured against earnings that were flattered by an accounting event, and that the business is being converted into something structurally worse.

Start with the flattery. Our screener reports earnings per share up 63.7% year on year, a three-year earnings growth rate of 44.9%, a 33.6% net margin and a margin "2.21 standard deviations above its historical peak". Nearly all of that comes from the first quarter of 2025, where reported operating income of RMB 4,836 million exceeded that quarter's entire gross profit of RMB 3,242 million by RMB 1,594 million. Only a large non-operating gain can do that. Strip it and the 2025 net margin is roughly 26-27%, not 33.6%, and the growth rate collapses. The screener's 57% gross margin and its "expanding" tag are also wrong - the quarterly filings show 44.1%, 44.4%, 43.5% and 44.2%, essentially flat, with one corrupt data point inflating the annual figure. The "Buffett fair value" of HK$80 that falls out of those inputs is therefore built on sand, and the two models that use normalised rather than extrapolated earnings agree: the earnings-power value says the stock is roughly fairly priced today and the owner-earnings model gives it about 6%.

Then the deceleration. Revenue grew 6.7% in the first quarter of 2026 and 5.8% in the second, and the second quarter already includes a partial period of newly acquired Ximalaya revenue. Allow for even a modest contribution and organic growth was close to flat - against a music segment that grew 22.9% in 2025. Net income grew only 2.6% on revenue up 5.8%. The market agreed with that reading on the day: the New York shares fell nearly 12% on 2026-08-11 and China Renaissance cut the stock to hold on 2026-08-12.

Then the margin. For two years management promised "the cost growth is always lower than the revenue growth". On 2026-08-11 the chief financial officer guided the other way: gross margin "decreasing slightly year-over-year", operating expenses up, and "net margin for the whole year will go down slightly". That is not a one-quarter wobble, it is the arithmetic of the mix shift. Concerts, merchandise and artist management are lower-margin, more working-capital-intensive and far more hit-dependent than a subscription, and management concedes the "initial stage" dilution without ever quantifying it or dating its end.

Then the capital allocation. Goodwill jumped RMB 9.3 billion and total debt went from RMB 4.8 billion to RMB 16.9 billion in a single quarter to buy a business management itself says carries a "higher sales and marketing cost ratio", and the company then raised a further US$1,000 million of notes on 2026-09-10 on top of RMB 44 billion of cash and deposits. Meanwhile the US$400 million of buyback did not shrink the share count at all: weighted diluted shares were 1,551 million a year ago and 1,556 million in the latest quarter. Shareholders paid for the repurchase and received no reduction in their share of the company.

And the information. From the first quarter of 2026 the company stopped disclosing paying subscribers and average revenue per paying user quarterly (announced 2026-03-17), one quarter before organic growth stalled, and it does not break out Ximalaya. An outside investor can no longer audit the core engine between annual reports. The bear confirmation is specific: a third-quarter print on 2026-11-17 showing revenue growth at or below the second quarter's with Ximalaya now fully consolidated, gross margin below about 43%, or further cash deployed into acquisitions.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market has flipped sides over the past three months, and it is worth being precise about it.

First, what the street has right and our own screener has wrong. Consensus for the quarter being reported on 2026-11-17 is US$0.22 of earnings per American share on about US$1.36 billion of revenue, which is roughly RMB 9.1 billion and about 7% growth on the RMB 8,463 million of a year earlier. That is a sensible number and it is mostly acquisition arithmetic: with the audio business consolidated for a full quarter, 7% reported growth is consistent with organic growth of only one or two percent. The street is not asleep here. Our own feed is the thing that is asleep: it reports a 57% gross margin that is "expanding", earnings per share up 63.7%, and a margin 2.21 standard deviations above its historical peak. All three are artifacts - the gross-margin series contains one impossible data point (gross profit of RMB 7,569 million on revenue of RMB 7,745 million), and the earnings growth comes from a single non-operating gain in the first quarter of 2025 large enough that reported operating income exceeded that quarter's whole gross profit. Anyone trading the 116% margin of safety our screener prints is trading an accounting event.

Second, what the street still has wrong, and it is a balance-sheet point rather than an earnings point. The published target range on the American shares is US$10 to US$15 with a consensus of US$12.50, which is about HK$39 to HK$59 per Hong Kong share. Those targets are built from earnings multiples and mostly ignore the cash. Management's own statement on 2026-08-11 - cash plus short-term plus long-term deposits of RMB 44 billion, "almost 40% of our current market cap" - means that on the lower targets the market is implicitly valuing the entire operating business, with its RMB 10 billion of annual operating profit, at something close to RMB 55 billion. That is the mispricing we think is real, and it is why our base case of HK$43 does not need the growth story to re-accelerate to work.

Third, where we disagree with the bulls. The street still largely treats the margin decline as transitional - the "initial stage" framing management has used on four consecutive calls. We think the mix shift into concerts, merchandise and artist management is permanent and permanently lower-margin, so gross profit will keep growing more slowly than revenue. That is why our multiple is 12.5 times rather than the high-teens a re-accelerating subscription compounder would deserve.
forcing_function:
The hard date is 2026-11-17: third-quarter 2026 results, announced by the company on 2026-10-13 and still unreported as of 2026-11-09. It is the forcing event for a specific reason. Since the first quarter of 2026 the company no longer publishes paying-subscriber counts or average revenue per paying user quarterly - that disclosure was withdrawn on 2026-03-17 in favour of an annual total-paying-users figure - and it does not break out the acquired audio business. So consolidated revenue growth and gross margin are now the only instruments an outside investor has, and 2026-11-17 is the first time we see them with the acquisition fully in the base. A print at or above 5% revenue growth with gross margin within about 1.5 points of a year earlier resolves the doubt in our favour and makes this a straightforward purchase; revenue down year on year, gross margin more than 3 points lower, or a swing into net debt breaks it.

Two further dates matter but are not decisive. Full-year results, due around March 2027, will carry the only annual paying-user disclosure the company now gives, which is the one remaining direct read on the subscription engine. And a new buyback authorisation, flagged as "preparing for another round" on 2026-08-11, would be the clearest signal that the cash is going back to shareholders rather than into more acquisitions - the question the 2026-11-17 call should be pressed on, given US$1,000 million of notes were raised in September on top of RMB 44 billion of cash and deposits.
valley_of_death:
The risky window is the next three to nine months, and most of it is self-inflicted rather than macro.

The immediate item is the report on 2026-11-17. It is the first quarter with the acquired audio business consolidated for a full period, which mechanically lifts revenue and mechanically dilutes gross margin - management has already said the acquired business carries a "higher sales and marketing cost ratio". A print that shows the reported revenue line looking better while the gross-profit line looks worse is the most likely single outcome, and it is an awkward one for a stock that has just risen 11% in a week.

The second item is guidance drift. On 2026-03-17 management guided 2026 gross margin flat to slightly lower and net margin "similar". By 2026-08-11 that had become "decreasing slightly year-over-year" and "net margin for the whole year will go down slightly". The fourth quarter is seasonally the heaviest for concerts and merchandise - the lowest-margin revenue in the mix - so the margin pressure peaks exactly when the annual number is set.

The third item is the cost of the new capital structure. Total debt went from RMB 4.8 billion to RMB 16.9 billion between 2026-03-31 and 2026-06-30, and the company then closed US$1,000 million of notes on 2026-09-10. Cash interest expense now runs against interest income on a deposit pile that is being drawn down for acquisitions - so the "clean earnings" we capitalise and the reported earnings will converge in the wrong direction for a few quarters.

The fourth item is goodwill. RMB 29.8 billion of it sits on a balance sheet with RMB 78.3 billion of equity, RMB 9.3 billion of it added in one quarter. If the acquired business misses its plan, the write-down lands in the same window.

And the fifth is simply the tape. The current regime read is an unfriendly one for anything that needs a benign backdrop: a December rate rise is roughly 85% priced on 3.7% headline inflation, the lowest-rated part of the credit market is still stressed with the gap between the weakest and second-weakest tiers above 1,100 basis points, and Brent crude settled above $110 for seven straight sessions in late October. This stock already demonstrated its beta to that kind of market - from HK$86.45 to HK$30.36 inside twelve months. What it does not have is any dependence on rate cuts, which the current regime specifically penalises; nothing in our thesis needs the Federal Reserve to help.
positioning_washout:
Forced-selling pressure here is modest and, unusually, the biggest mechanical flow runs the other way.

This is not a yield-holder base facing a dividend cut, and there is no pivot that would force an income fund to liquidate. The free float is about 73% of the American shares, with the balance held by the parent group, so there is no overhang from a departing control holder either. The company itself has been the marginal buyer: US$400 million of repurchases completed in the second quarter of 2026 alone, inside a US$1 billion programme, with another round "being prepared" as of 2026-08-11. That is a standing bid, not a seller.

The real risk is not mechanical but factor-driven - a sector or style sell-off rather than anything specific to the company. This is a Chinese internet platform with a dual listing in Hong Kong and New York, and it trades with that complex: the 57% fall from HK$86.45 to the HK$30.36 low over the past year was not caused by the company's own results, which grew throughout. A renewed de-rating of China platform assets, or a reversal of the trade truce that was extended to 10 January, would take the price down regardless of the 2026-11-17 print. The mirror image is what we have just watched: the shares rose about 11% in five sessions to 2026-11-09 on no company news at all, which tells you how much of the price is sector flow rather than fundamentals.

One quieter point about the buyback deserves flagging, because it affects what the forced bid is actually worth to shareholders. Despite US$400 million spent, the weighted diluted share count has not fallen - 1,551 million American shares a year ago, 1,556 million in the latest quarter. Share-based compensation is absorbing the entire repurchase. The buyback supports the price while it is running; it is not compounding value per share.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for proof: we buy once the third-quarter 2026 report confirms revenue growth at or above about 5% with gross margin holding and net cash intact, due 2026-11-17.

This is the same answer we gave last week and the week before, and we are deliberately not changing it. Nothing dated has happened to the business since our 2026-11-02 look: the only announcements on file are the reporting date itself (confirmed 2026-10-13) and the US$1,000 million notes that closed 2026-09-10, both of which we already knew. What has changed is the price - HK$33.50 to HK$37.16 at the close of 2026-11-09, about 11% in five sessions, with no company news behind it and the biggest single day on 2026-11-05. A price move is not evidence about a business, and we are not going to re-argue the case because the market got cheerful.

What we think is going on here is worth stating plainly, because our own screener is actively misleading on this name. The feed shows a 116% margin of safety, a 57% gross margin that is expanding, and earnings up 64%. All three are wrong. The gross-margin series contains one arithmetically impossible data point, and the earnings growth comes from a single non-operating gain in the first quarter of 2025 - a quarter where reported operating income was larger than the entire quarter's gross profit, which only an accounting gain can produce. Clean up the numbers and this is a business with roughly 44% gross margins, 34% operating margins, about RMB 8 billion of genuine annual earnings and RMB 13.8 billion of net cash. That is a good business at a fair-to-cheap price, not a stock trading at half its worth.

The part of the story we do believe, and which the market is still underweighting, is structural. Group revenue looked flat from 2021 to 2024 because two businesses inside it were cancelling each other out: online music compounded at about 29% a year to RMB 26.7 billion while the old live-streaming business collapsed by two-thirds to about RMB 5.3 billion. That drag is now only about 15% of revenue, so it has almost run its course. On top of that sits a balance sheet management itself values at close to 40% of the market capitalisation once longer-dated deposits are counted. Our base case values the operating business at 12.5 times clean earnings and adds net cash, which gives about HK$43 a share - comfortably inside the range the independent models produce (earnings-power value around HK$36, discounted cash flow around HK$48-52) and nowhere near the HK$80 that falls out of extrapolating flattered earnings.

The reason we are waiting is the quarter to 2026-06-30. Revenue grew 5.8% and net income 2.6%, and that quarter already contained part of a newly acquired audio business - so organic growth was close to flat, against a music segment that grew 22.9% the year before. Management also walked its own margin guidance down between March and August, and it withdrew quarterly subscriber disclosure in March, one quarter before the slowdown appeared. One soft quarter does not break a thesis, but it does mean the thesis is in doubt until the next print, and the company has removed every instrument we could use to check it in the meantime except consolidated revenue and gross margin. That makes 2026-11-17 not a trading event but the only available test, and it is seven days away - there is no case for pre-empting it.

Two honest marks against the position before anyone sizes it. First, the discount has narrowed to the point where it no longer clears our bar: at HK$37.16 the gap up to our HK$43 base case is smaller than the gap down to our HK$29.50 adverse case, which is why even a clean print may not make this a purchase at this price. Second, and we want to be clear rather than flattering about this, the apparent cheapness against Spotify, Warner and Universal is mostly shared sector risk rather than a mispricing we have uniquely found - China's other listed music-streaming business trades cheaper than TME on earnings, on sales and on cash flow today. We are being paid for China platform risk here. The genuinely company-specific asset is the cash, and the genuinely company-specific question is whether management keeps returning it or keeps spending it on acquisitions. bull_thesis:

But the company's segment disclosure shows two opposite businesses inside that flat line. Online music services (subscriptions and advertising) grew from RMB 12.5 billion in 2022 to RMB 26.7 billion in 2025, compounding at about 29% a year. Over the same period the old live-streaming and virtual-gifting business shrank from roughly RMB 15.9 billion to roughly RMB 5.3 billion, a two-thirds collapse under China's 2021 crackdown on tipping. The shrinking business is now only about 15% of revenue, so the drag that suppressed reported growth for three years is nearly exhausted, and group growth should converge upward toward the music engine rather than downward. On the 2026-08-11 call the company confirmed it "already completed USD 400 million share buyback" in the quarter and is "preparing for another round".

The shares are roughly 57% below their 52-week high of HK$86.45, at about 11 times trailing earnings and under 11 times once net cash is stripped out, for a business with 44% gross margins, 34% operating margins and the Tencent group's distribution behind it. macro_fit_note: Two parts of the backdrop pull in opposite directions, so we call it neutral and treat it as context rather than a reason. The debt-cycle read is a disciplined one - positive real long-term rates being imposed and holding, which punishes long-dated stories and rewards cash generated now, over an expected horizon of about 18 months - and that suits this company well: it already produces roughly RMB 11 billion of operating cash a year against a market value near RMB 98 billion and holds net cash rather than needing to refinance. Against that, the growth-and-inflation reading is reflationary (growth accelerating with inflation still hot or sticky, real output up about 3.4% annualised), and this is a business whose margins historically did not hold up in an inflationary stretch: its gross margin fell about 4 percentage points, from 34.1% to 30.1%, through the 2021-22 inflation, with operating margin down 6 points. On pass-through, the latest call gives us no comfort: on 2026-08-11 management guided gross margin "decreasing slightly year-over-year" and said "our net margin for the whole year will go down slightly" while sales expenses rise - costs are being absorbed, not passed on.
